submodules.title: 1. What Is Risk?
submodules.intro: Is risk only about losing money, or something more?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: WHAT IS RISK?
Every investment carries risk, which is the chance that the result will be different from what you hoped, usually worse. Risk is not something to avoid completely. It is something to understand, measure and keep to a level you can live with. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
A share that falls 50% needs to rise 100% just to get back to where it started.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: TYPES OF RISK
• Market risk: the whole market falls and takes most shares down with it.
• Company risk: something goes wrong at one business.
• Inflation risk: prices rise, so the same money buys less over time.
• Liquidity risk: you cannot sell quickly at a fair price.
• Concentration risk: too much money sits in one share or one sector.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: RISK AND RETURN
• Higher possible return usually comes with higher risk. Nobody can offer high returns with no risk.
• Volatility is how much a price swings up and down. Big swings feel uncomfortable even when the price later recovers.
• Drawdown = (peak - low) ÷ peak x 100. It shows the worst fall from a high point.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: THE RECOVERY TRAP
Losses are harder to repair than they look. After a fall of x%, the gain needed to recover is bigger than x%. A 20% fall needs a 25% gain. A 50% fall needs a 100% gain. This is why avoiding big losses matters so much.

🍕 MINI CASE: A FALL AND THE CLIMB BACK
The fictional Sundar Foods Ltd peaks at ₹200 and falls to ₹150. The drawdown is (200 - 150) ÷ 200 x 100 = 25%. To get back to ₹200 from ₹150, it needs to rise 50 ÷ 150 x 100 = 33.3%. Aarav says, 'It fell 25%, so it only needs 25% back.' Meera shows him the sum. The climb back is always steeper than the fall.

🧪 TRY IT: HOW STEEP IS THE CLIMB?
A fictional share falls from ₹100 to ₹50. What is the drawdown, and what gain is needed to return to ₹100?
(Answer: the drawdown is (100 - 50) ÷ 100 x 100 = 50%. To go from ₹50 to ₹100 it needs 50 ÷ 50 x 100 = 100%.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Risk is the chance of a worse result than you hoped for, and it comes in several kinds. Measure it with drawdown, remember that big losses are hard to repair, and only take risk you can live with.

quiz.question: Which risk means you cannot sell quickly at a fair price?
quiz.explanation: Liquidity risk is the difficulty of selling quickly without a bad price.

quiz.question: A share falls from ₹500 to ₹400. What is the drawdown?
After a 20% fall, what gain is needed to recover?
quiz.explanation: 100 falls to 80, and 80 must rise by 20 ÷ 80 = 25% to reach 100.

quiz.question: What is the usual link between risk and return?
options: Higher possible return usually comes with higher risk
High returns come with no risk
Lower risk always means higher return
quiz.explanation: Investments that offer more possible reward usually carry more risk.

quiz.question: What is inflation risk?
options: Prices rise so your money buys less over time
quiz.explanation: Inflation reduces what a rupee can buy.

submodules.title: 2. Diversification
submodules.intro: Why do investors say 'don't put all your eggs in one basket'?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: DIVERSIFICATION
Diversification means spreading your money across different investments so that one bad result does not ruin everything. It does not remove risk, and it does not promise profit. It reduces the damage from any single surprise. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
Most of the benefit of diversifying across shares often comes from the first 15 to 25 holdings, so owning 100 does not make a portfolio five times safer.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: TWO KINDS OF RISK
• Company-specific risk: one business has a fire, a fraud or poor results. Diversification can reduce this a lot.
• Market-wide risk: everything falls together because of a crisis or a rate shock. Diversification across shares alone cannot remove this.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: WAYS TO DIVERSIFY
• Across many companies.
• Across sectors such as banks, IT, FMCG, pharma and energy.
• Across asset classes such as shares, debt, gold and cash.
• Across time, by investing in parts instead of all at once.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: THE LIMITS
• Too many holdings (over-diversification) makes a portfolio hard to follow and dilutes your best ideas.
• Owning many shares from one sector is not real diversification.
• A single fund can already hold dozens of shares, so check what you own before adding more.

🍕 MINI CASE: ONE BASKET OR TEN
Aarav puts ₹1,00,000 into one fictional company, and it falls 40%. He loses ₹40,000. Meera spreads ₹1,00,000 equally over 10 fictional companies, ₹10,000 each. One of them also falls 40%, so she loses 10,000 x 0.4 = ₹4,000, which is 4% of her portfolio. Same bad news, very different damage.

🧪 TRY IT: SPREAD IT OUT
A fictional portfolio of ₹50,000 is split equally across 5 shares. One falls 50% and the others do not move. What is the loss in rupees and as a percentage of the portfolio?
(Answer: each share is ₹10,000, so the loss is 10,000 x 0.5 = ₹5,000. That is 5,000 ÷ 50,000 x 100 = 10% of the portfolio.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Diversification limits the damage from any one mistake or surprise. It cannot remove market-wide risk, and more holdings is not always better.

quiz.question: What does diversification mean?
quiz.explanation: Diversification spreads risk across several holdings.

quiz.question: ₹1,00,000 sits in one share that falls 40%. What is the loss?
₹1,00,000 is split equally over 10 shares and one falls 40%. What is the portfolio loss?
quiz.explanation: The share held ₹10,000 and lost ₹4,000, which is 4% of the portfolio.

quiz.question: Which risk can diversification across shares NOT remove?
quiz.explanation: When the whole market falls, most shares fall together.

quiz.question: Why can owning too many holdings be a problem?
options: It is hard to follow and dilutes your best ideas
quiz.explanation: Over-diversification adds effort and little extra safety.

submodules.title: 3. Asset Allocation
submodules.intro: How should money be split between shares, debt and gold?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: ASSET ALLOCATION
Asset allocation is how you divide your money between asset classes such as shares, debt, gold and cash. It is often said to matter more for a portfolio's ups and downs than picking individual shares. The right mix depends on your goal, your time horizon and how much of a fall you can tolerate. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
Different asset classes often behave differently, so when shares are weak, debt or gold may hold up better, though this is a tendency and not a promise.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: THE MAIN ASSET CLASSES
• Equity (shares): higher possible growth with large swings.
• Debt (bonds, debt funds, fixed deposits): lower swings and lower possible growth.
• Gold: a different pattern of movement, with no income.
• Cash: safe and available, but inflation slowly eats its value.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: WHAT SHAPES YOUR MIX
• Goal: money needed in 1 year should not sit in shares.
• Time horizon: a longer horizon gives more time to recover from falls.
• Risk tolerance: how you feel and behave when your portfolio drops 20%.
• A rough rule of '100 minus your age in shares' is only a starting idea, never a fixed rule.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: PORTFOLIO RETURN
A portfolio's return is each asset's return multiplied by its weight, then added up. Weights must add up to 100%.

🍕 MINI CASE: A MIX IN NUMBERS
Meera's fictional simulator portfolio is 60% equity, 30% debt and 10% gold. In one year, equity gives +10%, debt +6% and gold +4%. Portfolio return = 0.6 x 10 + 0.3 x 6 + 0.1 x 4 = 6 + 1.8 + 0.4 = 8.2%. Aarav asks why she holds the slower assets. Meera says they soften the falls when equity has a bad year.

🧪 TRY IT: WEIGHTED RETURN
A fictional portfolio is 50% equity, 40% debt and 10% gold. The year's returns are +12%, +5% and -2%. What is the portfolio return?
(Answer: 0.5 x 12 + 0.4 x 5 + 0.1 x (-2) = 6 + 2 - 0.2 = 7.8%.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Your mix of assets, shaped by your goal, time horizon and comfort with falls, drives much of your result. There is no single best mix, so choose one you can stick with.

quiz.question: What is asset allocation?
options: How money is divided between asset classes
quiz.explanation: It is the split between shares, debt, gold, cash and so on.

quiz.question: Weights 60/30/10 with returns 10%, 6% and 4%. What is the portfolio return?
Which asset class usually swings the most?
quiz.explanation: Equities usually have the biggest ups and downs.

quiz.question: Why can a longer time horizon allow more equity?
options: There is more time to recover from falls
quiz.explanation: A longer horizon gives time for temporary falls to heal.

quiz.question: Is '100 minus your age in shares' a fixed rule?
options: No, it is only a rough starting idea
quiz.explanation: Your goal and comfort with risk matter more than any formula.

submodules.title: 4. Correlation and Hidden Concentration
submodules.intro: Is a portfolio really diversified if everything moves together?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: CORRELATION AND HIDDEN CONCENTRATION
Owning many things is not the same as being diversified. What matters is whether your holdings move together. Correlation measures that. Two holdings that move in lockstep give you the risk of one. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
In sharp market crashes, many holdings that normally move differently suddenly fall together, which is why correlations tend to rise exactly when you want protection.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: WHAT CORRELATION MEANS
• It runs from -1 to +1.
• +1: the two move together perfectly.
• 0: no clear link.
• -1: they move in opposite directions.
• Low or negative correlation is what makes diversification work.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: HIDDEN CONCENTRATION
• Five bank shares are one bet on banking, not five separate bets.
• A share and a fund that holds the same share overlap.
• Several companies with the same big customer or the same raw material share one risk.
• Check sector weights and fund holdings, not only the number of names.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: CAUTION
Correlations change over time. A mix that looked well spread in calm months can behave like one big bet in a crisis, so look for different drivers of risk, not just different names.

🍕 MINI CASE: FIVE SHARES, ONE BET
Aarav holds five fictional shares of ₹20,000 each, all from banking, a ₹1,00,000 portfolio. Banking falls 10% and he loses 5 x 2,000 = ₹10,000, or 10%. Meera also holds five shares of ₹20,000, each from a different sector. If only one sector falls 10%, she loses ₹2,000, which is 2% of her portfolio. Both own five shares, but only one is truly spread out.

🧪 TRY IT: FIND THE CONCENTRATION
A fictional ₹80,000 portfolio holds four shares of ₹20,000 each. Three of them are IT companies. If the IT sector falls 10% and the other share stays flat, what is the loss in rupees and as a percentage of the portfolio?
(Answer: IT holdings are 3 x 20,000 = ₹60,000. The loss is 60,000 x 0.1 = ₹6,000, which is 6,000 ÷ 80,000 x 100 = 7.5% of the portfolio.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Real diversification means holdings that do not all move together. Look at sectors and overlaps, not just the number of names.

quiz.question: A correlation of +1 means the two holdings...
quiz.explanation: +1 is perfect movement in the same direction.

quiz.question: A correlation of -1 means the two holdings...
quiz.explanation: -1 is perfect movement in opposite directions.

quiz.question: Is a portfolio of ten banking shares well diversified?
options: It depends on the colour of the chart
No, they share one sector risk
quiz.explanation: Same-sector shares tend to move together.

quiz.question: ₹80,000 is spread over four equal shares. Three are IT and IT falls 10%. What is the portfolio loss?
What often happens to correlations in a sharp market crash?
options: They tend to rise as many things fall together
quiz.explanation: In a crash, many assets fall at once.

submodules.title: 5. Position Sizing
submodules.intro: How much should you put into a single idea?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: POSITION SIZING
Position sizing means deciding how much money goes into one trade or one share. Even good ideas fail, so the size of each bet decides whether a bad run is an annoyance or a disaster. A simple tool is to risk only a small fixed percentage of your capital on each idea. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
A string of 10 losses in a row, painful as it sounds, happens to many traders at some point. Position size decides whether they survive it.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: THE FIXED-RISK METHOD
• Decide the most you will lose on one idea, often 1% of capital or less.
• Risk per share = entry price - stop-loss price.
• Number of shares = amount you are willing to risk ÷ risk per share.
• Position value = number of shares x entry price.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: WHY SMALL RISK PER TRADE
• Losses compound. With 1% risk per trade, 10 losses in a row leave about 90.4% of your capital, a fall of about 9.6%.
• With 10% risk per trade, 10 losses in a row leave only about 34.9%, a fall of about 65%.
• Small risk keeps you in the game long enough to learn.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: OTHER LIMITS TO SET
• A cap on any single position, such as no more than 10% of the portfolio.
• A cap on how much is risked across all open trades at once.
• Smaller size when you are less sure or when a share is very volatile.

🍕 MINI CASE: SIZING A SIMULATOR TRADE
Meera has ₹1,00,000 in her simulator and risks 1%, which is ₹1,000. She plans to buy a fictional share at ₹250 with a stop-loss at ₹240. Risk per share is 250 - 240 = ₹10. Shares = 1,000 ÷ 10 = 100. The position value is 100 x 250 = ₹25,000, which is 25% of her capital. She checks her own 10% cap per position and decides to buy 40 shares instead, a value of ₹10,000.

🧪 TRY IT: SIZE THE TRADE
A fictional account has ₹2,00,000 and risks 1% per trade. The plan is entry ₹500 and stop-loss ₹480. How many shares, and what is the position value?
(Answer: the risk amount is ₹2,000 and the risk per share is ₹20, so shares = 2,000 ÷ 20 = 100. The position value is 100 x 500 = ₹50,000, which is 25% of the account.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Decide how much you can lose before you decide how much to buy. Small, fixed risk per idea keeps you alive through losing streaks.

quiz.question: What is position sizing?
options: Deciding how much to put into one idea
quiz.explanation: It decides how big each position is.

quiz.question: Capital is ₹1,00,000 and you risk 1% per trade. How much is risked?
Risk amount ₹1,000, entry ₹250, stop ₹240. How many shares?
quiz.explanation: Risk per share is 10, so 1,000 ÷ 10 = 100 shares.

quiz.question: Risking 10% per trade, about how much capital is left after 10 straight losses?
quiz.explanation: 0.9 multiplied ten times is about 0.349, so about 35% is left.

quiz.question: Why risk only a small percentage per trade?
options: It helps you survive losing streaks
quiz.explanation: Small risk keeps losses manageable.

submodules.title: 6. Mutual Funds
submodules.intro: How can many people invest together in one basket?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: MUTUAL FUNDS
A mutual fund collects money from many investors and invests it in a mix of shares, bonds or other assets, run by a professional fund manager. Each investor owns units of the fund. In India, mutual funds are regulated by SEBI. Real investing needs a parent or guardian for anyone under 18. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
Mutual fund units are priced once a day, after the market closes, using a number called NAV.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: HOW A FUND WORKS
• You buy units, and the fund invests the pooled money.
• NAV (Net Asset Value) = (value of the fund's assets - liabilities) ÷ number of units.
• Units bought = amount invested ÷ NAV.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: MAIN TYPES
• Equity funds: invest mostly in shares, with higher risk and higher possible growth.
• Debt funds: invest in bonds and similar instruments, usually with smaller swings, but not risk-free.
• Hybrid funds: a mix of equity and debt.
• Index funds: copy an index like the Nifty 50.
• Direct and regular plans: the same fund, but direct plans have lower costs because they pay no distributor commission.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: CAUTIONS
• A low NAV does not mean a fund is cheap. NAV level says nothing about value.
• Past returns do not guarantee future returns.
• Read the fund's riskometer, holdings and costs before choosing.

🍕 MINI CASE: READING A NAV
A fictional fund has assets of ₹5,25,00,000 and liabilities of ₹25,00,000, with 25,00,000 units. Net assets are ₹5,00,00,000, so NAV = 5,00,00,000 ÷ 25,00,000 = ₹200. An investment of ₹10,000 buys 10,000 ÷ 200 = 50 units. Aarav says a ₹20 NAV fund must be cheaper. Meera explains that NAV alone says nothing about value.

🧪 TRY IT: FIND THE NAV
A fictional fund has net assets of ₹60,00,000 and 3,00,000 units. What is the NAV, and how many units does ₹5,000 buy?
(Answer: NAV = 60,00,000 ÷ 3,00,000 = ₹20. Units = 5,000 ÷ 20 = 250 units.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
A mutual fund pools many investors' money under a professional manager. Understand NAV, fund type and costs, and remember that a low NAV does not mean a bargain.

quiz.question: What is a mutual fund?
options: A pool of many investors' money invested together
quiz.explanation: Many investors pool money, and a manager invests it.

quiz.question: A fund has net assets of ₹5,00,00,000 and 25,00,000 units. What is the NAV?
NAV is ₹200. How many units does ₹10,000 buy?
Who regulates mutual funds in India?
quiz.explanation: SEBI regulates mutual funds in India.

quiz.question: Is a fund with a lower NAV cheaper?
options: No, NAV level says nothing about value
quiz.explanation: What matters are holdings, returns and costs, not the NAV number.

submodules.title: 7. ETFs and Index Funds
submodules.intro: What if you just want to follow the market instead of beating it?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: ETFS AND INDEX FUNDS
An index fund and an ETF both try to copy an index, such as the Nifty 50, instead of trying to beat it. They hold the same shares as the index in the same proportions. This keeps costs low and the idea simple. Real investing needs a parent or guardian for anyone under 18. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
A fund that simply copies an index needs no star stock picker, which is a big reason its fees can be so low.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: THE TWO FORMS
• Index fund: a mutual fund that tracks an index. You buy and sell units at NAV through the fund house or a platform.
• ETF (Exchange Traded Fund): tracks an index too, but trades on the exchange like a share, so you need a demat and trading account.
• ETF prices move through the day, and a small gap between the ETF price and its underlying value can appear.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: TRACKING DIFFERENCE
• A fund cannot copy its index perfectly. Costs and small timing gaps cause a difference.
• Tracking difference = fund return - index return. It is usually a small negative number close to the fund's cost.
• Tracking error is how much that gap wobbles over time.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: WHAT TO CHECK
• Expense ratio: lower is better for the same index.
• Liquidity of an ETF: check that there is enough trading and a small bid-ask gap.
• The index itself: a Nifty 50 fund and a small-cap fund carry very different risk.

🍕 MINI CASE: TRACKING THE INDEX
A fictional Nifty 50 index fund earns 11.8% in a year while the index returns 12%. The tracking difference is 11.8 - 12 = -0.2 percentage points, close to the fund's yearly cost. Meera compares two ETFs on the same index and picks the one with the smaller cost and the tighter bid-ask gap. Aarav notes that copying the index means he gets the market's risk, including its falls.

🧪 TRY IT: MEASURE THE GAP
A fictional index returns 10% and a fund tracking it returns 9.7%. What is the tracking difference?
(Answer: 9.7 - 10 = -0.3 percentage points.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Index funds and ETFs follow a market at low cost. They give market returns and market risk, so pick the index, the cost and the liquidity with care.

quiz.question: What does an index fund try to do?
quiz.explanation: It tracks an index such as the Nifty 50.

quiz.question: How is an ETF different from an index fund?
options: It trades on the exchange like a share
quiz.explanation: An ETF is bought and sold on the exchange during market hours.

quiz.question: An index returns 12% and a fund returns 11.8%. What is the tracking difference?
What do you need to buy an ETF on the exchange?
quiz.explanation: ETFs trade like shares, so a demat and trading account is needed.

quiz.question: Does an index fund remove market risk?
options: No, it follows the market including its falls
quiz.explanation: It copies the index, so it shares the index's risk.

submodules.title: 8. SIP and Rupee Cost Averaging
submodules.intro: Does investing a fixed amount every month help?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: SIP AND RUPEE COST AVERAGING
A SIP (Systematic Investment Plan) invests a fixed amount at regular intervals, usually monthly, into a fund. It builds a habit, removes the pressure of timing the market and lets you start small. It does not guarantee profit. Real SIPs for anyone under 18 need a parent or guardian. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
A SIP buys more units when the price is low and fewer when it is high, without you having to decide anything.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: HOW IT WORKS
• Each month the same rupee amount buys units at that day's NAV.
• Low NAV means more units. High NAV means fewer units.
• Average cost per unit = total invested ÷ total units. This is called rupee cost averaging.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: WHAT IT DOES AND DOES NOT DO
• It helps with discipline and with avoiding big one-time timing mistakes.
• It does not prevent losses if the market keeps falling for a long time.
• It does not turn a bad fund into a good one.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: COMMON MISTAKES
• Stopping the SIP in panic after a fall, with no reason linked to your goal.
• Raising the amount beyond what the budget can bear.
• Watching the NAV every day and reacting to noise.

🍕 MINI CASE: THREE MONTHS OF SIP
Meera invests ₹5,000 a month in a fictional fund. NAV is ₹50 in month 1, ₹40 in month 2 and ₹50 in month 3. She buys 100, 125 and 100 units, 325 units in all, for ₹15,000. Average cost = 15,000 ÷ 325 = ₹46.15. The simple average of the three NAVs is (50 + 40 + 50) ÷ 3 = ₹46.67, so the SIP bought slightly cheaper than the average price.

🧪 TRY IT: COUNT THE UNITS
A fictional SIP invests ₹2,000 a month. NAV is ₹10, ₹8 and ₹10 in three months. How many units in total, and what is the average cost per unit?
(Answer: units = 200 + 250 + 200 = 650. Total invested is ₹6,000, so average cost = 6,000 ÷ 650 = ₹9.23.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
A SIP builds a regular habit and averages your buying price. It is a discipline tool, not a profit guarantee.

quiz.question: What is a SIP?
options: A fixed amount invested at regular intervals
quiz.explanation: A SIP invests the same amount on a regular schedule.

quiz.question: ₹5,000 is invested at NAV ₹40. How many units are bought?
A SIP buys 100, 125 and 100 units for ₹15,000 in total. How many units is that?
Does a SIP guarantee profit?
options: No, it does not remove market risk
quiz.explanation: A SIP is a method of investing and carries the fund's risk.

quiz.question: Which is a common SIP mistake?
options: Stopping in panic after a fall with no goal-based reason
Matching the amount to the budget
quiz.explanation: Panic stops break the discipline that makes a SIP work.

submodules.title: 9. Costs, Fees and the Long Run
submodules.intro: How can a small fee quietly eat a big part of your return?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: COSTS, FEES AND THE LONG RUN
Costs are one of the few things in investing that you can control. A fee of 1% sounds tiny, but it is charged every year on a growing amount of money, so over many years it adds up to a lot. Always check the cost before you invest. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
Because returns compound, a cost that looks tiny each year can take a noticeable chunk of your final amount over 20 or 30 years.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: COMMON COSTS
• Expense ratio (TER): the yearly fee of a fund as a % of its assets, taken out of the fund's returns.
• Exit load: a charge if you sell units within a set period.
• Brokerage and other charges when you buy or sell shares or ETFs.
• Taxes: they reduce what you keep, and Module 12 covers them.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: DIRECT VS REGULAR
• A direct plan has no distributor commission, so its expense ratio is lower than the regular plan of the same fund.
• The portfolio inside is the same. Only the cost differs.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: THE MATHS OF A FEE
• Net return = gross return - cost.
• Final value = amount x (1 + net return) raised to the number of years.
• Costs are certain, while returns are not, so keeping costs low is a sure gain.

🍕 MINI CASE: ONE PERCENT OVER TEN YEARS
Aarav and Meera each invest ₹1,00,000 for 10 years in funds that earn 10% before costs. Aarav's fund charges 1.5%, so his net return is 8.5%, and 1,00,000 x 1.085 to the power of 10 is about ₹2,26,098. Meera's fund charges 0.5%, so her net return is 9.5%, and 1,00,000 x 1.095 to the power of 10 is about ₹2,47,823. The 1% gap in cost costs Aarav about ₹21,725.

🧪 TRY IT: COUNT THE COST
A fictional fund earns 8% before costs and charges 1%. You invest ₹1,00,000 for 10 years. What is the value with the fee, and what is the value if there were no fee?
(Answer: with the fee, the net return is 7%, and 1,00,000 x 1.07 to the power of 10 is about ₹1,96,715. With no fee, 1,00,000 x 1.08 to the power of 10 is about ₹2,15,892. The fee costs about ₹19,177.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Costs compound just like returns do. Check the expense ratio and other charges before you invest, because lower cost is one of the few sure advantages.

quiz.question: What is an expense ratio?
options: The yearly fee of a fund as a % of its assets
quiz.explanation: It is the yearly running cost charged by the fund.

quiz.question: ₹1,00,000 grows at 9.5% a year for 10 years. About what is the final amount?
quiz.explanation: 1,00,000 x 1.095 to the power of 10 is about ₹2,47,823.

quiz.question: In the lesson, how much did the 1% higher fee cost over 10 years?
What is an exit load?
options: A charge for selling units within a set period
quiz.explanation: Exit loads apply if you sell too early.

quiz.question: Why is a direct plan usually cheaper than a regular plan?
quiz.explanation: Direct plans skip the distributor commission.

submodules.title: 10. Rebalancing
submodules.intro: What do you do when one part of your portfolio grows too big?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: REBALANCING
Over time, the assets that grow fastest take a larger share of your portfolio, so your risk drifts away from your plan. Rebalancing means bringing the weights back to your target. It is a simple way to manage risk, without having to guess the market. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
Rebalancing forces you to trim what has risen and add to what has lagged, which is the opposite of what excitement or fear usually tells you to do.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: WHY DRIFT HAPPENS
• Suppose you start with 60% equity and 40% debt.
• If equity rises faster, it might become 70% of the portfolio. You now hold more risk than you planned.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: WAYS TO REBALANCE
• Calendar method: check once or twice a year and reset to the target.
• Threshold method: rebalance when an asset is more than about 5 percentage points away from target.
• Cash-flow method: direct new money into the part that is below target, so you do not have to sell.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: COSTS TO WATCH
• Selling can mean brokerage, exit loads and taxes.
• Rebalancing too often adds cost without much benefit.
• Use new money first when you can.

🍕 MINI CASE: TRIMMING THE WINNER
Meera's fictional simulator portfolio starts at ₹1,00,000: ₹60,000 equity and ₹40,000 debt. Equity rises to ₹80,000 while debt stays at ₹40,000, so the total is ₹1,20,000 and equity is 80,000 ÷ 1,20,000 = 66.7%. Her target is 60%, which is 0.6 x 1,20,000 = ₹72,000. She sells ₹8,000 of equity and moves it to debt, giving ₹48,000 in debt.

🧪 TRY IT: REBALANCE IT
A fictional portfolio starts at ₹1,00,000 with a 50/50 split. Equity grows to ₹70,000 and debt stays at ₹50,000. What is the equity weight now, and how much equity must be sold to return to 50%?
(Answer: the total is ₹1,20,000 and equity is 70,000 ÷ 1,20,000 = 58.3%. The target is 50% of 1,20,000 = ₹60,000, so sell ₹10,000 of equity.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Rebalancing resets your risk to the level you chose. Pick a simple rule, mind the costs and use new money where possible.

submodules.title: 11. Measuring Performance
submodules.intro: How do you know whether your portfolio is really doing well?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: MEASURING PERFORMANCE
A rising portfolio is not always a good one. To judge it fairly, compare it with a benchmark, express growth per year, and look at how much risk was taken to get there. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
If a portfolio falls 50% and then rises 50%, it does not return to the start. It ends 25% lower.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: CAGR: GROWTH PER YEAR
• CAGR = (end value ÷ start value) raised to (1 ÷ number of years), minus 1.
• It shows the steady yearly growth that would give the same result.
• It lets you compare periods of different lengths.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: BENCHMARKS
• A benchmark is a fair yardstick such as the Nifty 50 for a large-company equity fund.
• Excess return = your return - benchmark return.
• If you cannot beat a simple index fund after costs, an index fund may be the easier choice.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: RETURN PER UNIT OF RISK
• A simple version: (return - risk-free rate) ÷ volatility. This is the idea behind the Sharpe ratio.
• A higher number means more return for the risk taken.
• Also watch the maximum drawdown, which is the worst fall from a peak.

🍕 MINI CASE: BEATING THE BENCHMARK
Meera's fictional portfolio grows from ₹1,00,000 to ₹1,61,051 in 5 years. Since 1.1 to the power of 5 is 1.61051, the CAGR is 10%. The Nifty gave 12% a year in the same period, so she lagged it by 2 percentage points. Next, portfolio A returns 12% with volatility of 15 and portfolio B returns 10% with volatility of 8, and the risk-free rate is 6%. A scores (12 - 6) ÷ 15 = 0.4 and B scores (10 - 6) ÷ 8 = 0.5. B earned more per unit of risk.

🧪 TRY IT: FIND THE CAGR
A fictional portfolio grows from ₹1,00,000 to ₹1,44,000 in 2 years. What is the CAGR?
(Answer: 1,44,000 ÷ 1,00,000 = 1.44, and the square root of 1.44 is 1.2, so the CAGR is 20%.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Judge a portfolio by yearly growth, against a fair benchmark and with the risk taken in mind, not by the final number alone.

submodules.title: 12. Your Portfolio Plan
submodules.intro: How do you turn everything into one written plan you can follow?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: YOUR PORTFOLIO PLAN
You now know about risk, diversification, asset allocation, correlation, position sizing, funds, SIPs, costs, rebalancing and measurement. This capstone puts them into one written plan. A written plan lets you decide calmly now, so you do not decide in a panic later. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
Many investors who write down their rules in advance find it easier to stay calm when markets fall, because the decision has already been made.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: THE PLAN CHECKLIST
1. Goal: what is the money for, and when is it needed?
2. Time horizon: money needed within 1 to 3 years should stay out of risky assets.
3. Risk limit: the largest fall you can accept without panicking.
4. Asset allocation: the target split, such as shares, debt and gold.
5. Position limits: the most in any single share, and the most risked per trade.
6. Costs: choose low-cost options where possible.
7. Rebalancing rule: calendar or threshold.
8. Review dates: when you will check progress and update the plan.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: BEFORE INVESTING
• Build an emergency fund first, often 3 to 6 months of expenses, kept safe and easy to reach.
• Do not invest money you cannot afford to see fall.
• Avoid borrowing to invest.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: WHAT TO AVOID
• Changing the plan after every headline.
• Chasing last year's best performer.
• Copying someone else's plan without checking your own goal and risk limit.
• Skipping reviews, or reviewing too often.

🍕 MINI CASE: MEERA'S SIMULATOR PLAN
Meera writes a plan for her ₹1,00,000 simulator account. Goal: practise for 3 months. Allocation: 50% index fund, 30% debt fund, 10% gold and 10% individual shares, which adds up to 100%. Limits: no single share above 10% of the account, which is ₹10,000, and no more than 1% risked per trade, which is ₹1,000. Rebalance if any part drifts more than 5 points from its target. She reviews it every month and shares it with her teacher.

🧪 TRY IT: WRITE YOUR OWN
Fill in all eight checklist lines for a goal of your choice, using simulator money. Then compute your emergency fund target: if monthly expenses are ₹20,000, what is 6 months of expenses?
(Answer: 6 x 20,000 = ₹1,20,000. Share your plan with a parent, teacher or guardian and review it with them.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
A written plan turns good ideas into repeatable rules. No plan guarantees profit, so practise on a simulator and involve a parent or guardian in any real money decision.
